definitions.definition: A mapping between two things that shows they have the same structure or pattern.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is an isomorphism to the actual tracks because the connections match up.

definitions.definition: A physical quantity that has a value at every point in space and time, but no direction.
definitions.example: Temperature is a scalar field because every point in a room has a temperature, but it doesn't point anywhere.

definitions.definition: A mathematical equation that describes how a scalar field (like a particle) moves through space and time.
definitions.example: It's like the rule that tells a wave on a string how to ripple, but for quantum fields.

definitions.definition: A way that one field interacts with another, named after physicist Hideki Yukawa.
definitions.example: Like two magnets that attract each other, but the force is carried by a particle.

definitions.definition: The idea that the total number of souls stays the same over time, unless God creates a new one.
definitions.example: Like the number of coins in a sealed jar stays the same unless you add or remove one.

definitions.definition: Living forever; never dying or being destroyed.
definitions.example: In stories, vampires are often said to be immortal because they don't age or die.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'image of God'; the belief that humans are made to reflect God's character.
definitions.example: Like a mirror that reflects your face, humans are meant to reflect God's love and creativity.

definitions.definition: The connection between a person's soul and their physical body during life.
definitions.example: Like a Wi-Fi connection between a phone and a computer—they're linked until you turn off the connection.

definitions.definition: When two things that were connected stop interacting with each other.
definitions.example: Unplugging a lamp from the wall—the lamp still exists, but it's no longer connected to electricity.

definitions.definition: The belief that after death, a person's body and soul will be reunited and live again.
definitions.example: In Christianity, Jesus rising from the tomb three days after his crucifixion.

definitions.definition: A distance that tells you how far a particle's quantum effects can spread; for a massless particle, it's infinite.
definitions.example: If you drop a pebble in a pond, the ripples spread out—the Compton wavelength is like the maximum distance those ripples can reach.

definitions.definition: Short for Quantum Field Theory, the physics framework that describes how particles and forces work at the smallest scales.
definitions.example: It's the rulebook for how tiny things like electrons and photons behave.

definitions.definition: Particles that have no intrinsic rotation (spin), like the Higgs boson.
definitions.example: Imagine a perfectly smooth ball that doesn't spin—that's like a spin-0 particle.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven wrong by an experiment or observation.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan proves it false.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or foundation that something is built on.
definitions.example: The canvas is the substrate for a painting—it's what holds the paint.

definitions.definition: Not able to be proven wrong, often because it's too vague or untestable.
definitions.example: The claim 'invisible unicorns live on the moon' is unfalsifiable because you can't check.

definitions.definition: A rule that says every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law (like energy being conserved).
definitions.example: If a dance move is the same when you turn around, that symmetry means something is conserved, like momentum.

definitions.definition: A flow of something (like charge) that doesn't change over time—it's always the same amount.
definitions.example: Water flowing through a pipe with no leaks—the amount of water per second stays constant.

definitions.definition: Cosmic Microwave Background—the faint glow left over from the Big Bang that fills the universe.
definitions.example: Like the afterglow of a fire that you can still see long after the flames are gone.

definitions.definition: The effective number of types of neutrinos (or similar particles) in the early universe, used to test new particles.
definitions.example: It's like counting how many different ingredients are in a soup by tasting it.

definitions.definition: The period between a person's death and their eventual resurrection, when the soul exists without a body.
definitions.example: Like a movie character who exists in a digital world after their body is destroyed, waiting to be put back into a new body.

definitions.definition: The belief that God creates each individual soul at the moment of conception or birth.
definitions.example: Like a baker making each cookie from scratch, rather than passing dough from one cookie to another.

definitions.definition: The belief that a child's soul is inherited from the parents, like their body is.
definitions.example: Like passing down a family recipe—the soul is 'handed down' from generation to generation.

definitions.definition: The idea that the simplest explanation (with the fewest assumptions) is usually the best one.
definitions.example: If you hear hoofbeats, it's more likely a horse than a zebra—the simpler answer is usually right.

definitions.definition: A theory that every known particle has a heavier 'superpartner' particle, which hasn't been found yet.
definitions.example: Like every character in a video game having a secret twin with different powers.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical particle that is the superpartner of the graviton (the particle that carries gravity).
definitions.example: If gravity had a shadowy twin particle, that would be the gravitino.

definitions.definition: The ability to choose between right and wrong and be responsible for those choices.
definitions.example: A person can decide to tell the truth or lie—that's moral agency. A rock can't choose.

definitions.definition: The size or strength of a wave, like how high a wave on the ocean gets.
definitions.example: Turning up the volume on a speaker increases the amplitude of the sound wave.

definitions.definition: The position of a wave in its cycle, like whether it's at a peak or a trough.
definitions.example: Two swings moving together are 'in phase'; if one is at the top while the other is at the bottom, they're 'out of phase'.

definitions.definition: Turning an idea into a precise, mathematical or logical form.
definitions.example: Turning a recipe written in plain English into a list of exact measurements and steps.

definitions.definition: A deep match between the patterns or relationships in two different systems.
definitions.example: The way a family tree shows relationships is structurally isomorphic to how a company's org chart shows who reports to whom.

definitions.definition: Relating to the end of the world or the final destiny of humanity.
definitions.example: Stories about the apocalypse or the final judgment are eschatological.

definitions.definition: A state or pattern that a system naturally moves toward over time.
definitions.example: A marble in a bowl always rolls to the bottom—the bottom is the attractor.

definitions.definition: A basic statement that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A property that appears when simple parts come together in a complex system, but isn't present in the parts alone.
definitions.example: Wetness emerges from many water molecules, but a single water molecule isn't wet.
